text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London kept modest gains by the close on scale-down manufacturer buying after Asian selling dried up, floor sources said. Benchmark September was traded between $1,805 and $1,835 per tonne before closing $39 up at $1,824 per tonne. Technically, analysts said the market was likely to continue base-building following the recent sharp downward move, before attempting another rally. On the upside, the $2,000 level basis September was seen as a psychological barrier. On the physical front, traders said business in Europe has dried up due to the summer lull and the tight Asian and Central American supplies.

Arabica futures in New York posted strong gains for the second straight day, bolstered by continued speculative buying, traders said. It was added sentiment is turning bullish again which also corresponds with the seasonal pattern which suggests the market typically bottoms out at this time of the year and works higher during non-freeze years. Renewed bullishness was sparked by a USDA attache report which showed a smaller Brazilian crop than the official USDA figure and on concerns about supply tightness in the months ahead due to only limited quantities of high quality coffee being available. Benchmark September rose 5.40 cents/lb on the day to 177.05 cents/lb, after ranging from 178.50 to 171.50. Spot July ended 5.50 cents/lb higher at 197.00 cents/lb, while the outer months closed up 0.75 to 4.20 cents/lb. UNITED STATES - After Wednesday's close, the CSCE reported stocks rose by 6,425 60-kg bags as of July 8, to 61,792 bags. An additional 41,163 bags were pending exchange approval, the CSCE added.

MEXICO - Mexico is targeting coffee output of 6 million 60-kg bags for the 1997/98 harvest, compared with 5.1 million bags harvested in the recently ended 1996/97 season, Mexican Coffee Council president Ruben Castillo said. Exports should reach about 5 million 60-kg bags for the 1996/97 season, compared to about 4.13 million bags as of the end of June, he told Reuters. Castillo said the goal was to increase production by 1 million bags each year until 2000, and let it stabilize at 8 million bags. He estimated Mexico will export all but about 1 million bags it consumes domestically per year. The expansion is based on an expected better use of coffee plantations, he said. Mexico will subsidize a new smaller variety of plant, so that coffee growers can cultivate more coffee plants in the same space. In Mexico the average ha has 1,340 plants, whereas modern coffee plantations have between 2,500 and 5,000 plants, Castillo added.

GERMANY ** - Coffee imports in March 1997 amounted to 1.176 million bags compared to 1.257 million bags in March 1996. This brought cumulative imports in the first quarter of 1997 (January/March) up to 3.780 million bags, up 18 per cent on the quantity imported in the like period the previous year. Total imports in 1996 reached 13.577 million bags against 12.897 million bags in 1995. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/March 1997 were Colombia (656,800 vs 810,600 bags), Brazil (634,200 vs 108,600 bags) and El Salvador (292,700 vs 252,700 bags).

Coffee exports in March 1997 amounted to 344,731 bags, up from 251,703 bags in March 1996. This brought cumulative exports in January/March 1997 up to 1.002 million bags compared to 839,406 bags in 1996. Total exports in 1996 amounted to 3.805 million bags against 3.238 million bags in 1995. German exports are mostly in the form of roast and ground with the Netherlands (80,300 vs 87,600 bags) and Belgium-Luxembourg (71,700 bags, unchanged) being the main markets.
